name: fine

attributes.attribute: gave English the word clan through its Gaelic
clans there often carried an attached sept

sources: Kelly, Fergus. A Guide to Early Irish Law. (Dublin: School of Celtic Studies, Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, 1988), 12-13.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Fine is the Irish term for a kin group, the seed of the later idea of a clan. English took clan from Scottish Gaelic, and the word points to shared blood rather than shared land. Old Irish clann named children and offspring before it named a whole line. The Latin planta, a plant or setting out, stands at its far root. Beside fine stood terms such as cenel and derbfine, while tuath leaned toward territory and people. In Scotland a clan often carried a sept whose tie to the founder sat distant or doubted. Warriors sickened of Concobar and left his kingdom. They went to serve queen Medb of Connacht. Medb then launched a war against him. Their struggle formed the basis of the epic Tain Bo Cuailnge.

okr.objective: Fine names the Irish kin group behind the clan, and the Tain legend shows kin politics at war.
key_results: English borrowed clan from Scottish Gaelic, and it marks kinship rather than territory.
Old Irish clann meant children and offspring before it named a wider line.
Terms such as cenel and derbfine stood beside fine, while tuath leaned toward territory.
Warriors left Concobar for Medb, and their war grounded the Tain Bo Cuailnge.
